PTC3567 · Data science study · October 2026

Living conditions and health resources in São Paulo

Socioeconomic profiles, public and non-public resources, and territorial context across 645 municipalities

What the data show

The analysis identifies 3 exploratory socioeconomic profiles across 645 municipalities. Non-SUS physician employment links are more strongly associated with income than SUS links. Demographic adjustment weakens these associations, while basic health unit density shows almost no remaining income association.

645municipalities
3exploratory profiles
0.34silhouette
0.97median refit ARI
  • Mean income has a Spearman correlation of 0.56 with non-SUS physician jobs per resident, versus 0.31 with SUS jobs.
  • After accounting for population, density and the share aged 65+, those correlations become 0.26 and 0.19.
  • The income association with basic health units per resident changes from -0.42 to -0.03 after the same adjustment.
  • Pooled infant mortality ranges from 12.64 in the lowest mean-income quartile to 10.69 in the highest, per 1,000 live births. The unweighted municipal income correlation is only -0.01.

These are descriptive municipal associations. Recorded resources do not establish effective access, service capacity or individual health risk.

Research question and data

Which socioeconomic profiles distinguish São Paulo municipalities, and how do SUS and non-SUS resources vary across them after considering demographic and territorial context?

SUS is Brazil’s public Unified Health System. “Non-SUS” is the source classification and should not be interpreted as a direct measure of insurance coverage or ownership.

RoleIndicatorsReference
Build profilesMedian household income per capita; literacy at age 15+; adverse sanitation shareIBGE census 2022

All joins use seven-digit IBGE identifiers. Totals, unique keys, positive denominators and percentage ranges are checked. Decimal commas and thousands separators are parsed explicitly. Each source file has a SHA-256 digest.

Adverse sanitation is the share of occupied permanent private households using rudimentary pits, ditches, rivers/lakes/sea, other forms, or having no toilet. Septic systems unconnected to a network are excluded from this proxy. The grouping is an analytical definition; it does not measure treatment quality or certify individual installations.

10 municipalities lack a physician record and 2 lack a nurse record. Missingness does not affect socioeconomic clustering. UBS totals are reported for all 645 municipalities. Hospital beds are reported for only 356 municipalities in 2024; missing bed rows remain unknown and beds are excluded from substantive comparisons. Ownership-component blanks in the UBS source are not interpreted as zero; only reported totals are used.

Profile construction and validation

The pipeline uses log median income, untransformed literacy and adverse sanitation, followed by z-score standardization. Each municipality has equal weight. K-means is fitted in this three-dimensional space; PCA is used for interpretation, with no dimensions discarded before clustering.

For each k from 2 to 6, the analysis fits K-means with 30 initializations, checks 10 seeds, compares Ward on the same standardized data, and refits scaling and K-means on 80 random subsamples containing 80% of municipalities. ARI compares the resulting assignments across all municipalities and separately among the excluded municipalities.

Selection rule: Among k=2..6 within 0.02 of maximum silhouette and >=30 towns per cluster, maximize the 10th-percentile full-pipeline refit ARI; break ties by smaller k. Exploratory heuristic, not preregistered. This rule is a transparent exploratory trade-off, not a hypothesis test or a universal threshold. Two profiles separate slightly better, while three offer stronger lower-tail stability; four provide additional detail but less consistent stability.

The selected model has median refit ARI 0.968, 10th-percentile ARI 0.934, and Ward agreement 0.653. The silhouette of 0.339 indicates overlap. The first principal component captures 64.8% of variance, consistent with a substantial continuous socioeconomic gradient.

Profile 1 combines lower income with much more frequent adverse sanitation. Profile 2 has intermediate income and literacy but substantially less adverse sanitation than Profile 1. Profile 3 combines higher income and literacy with lower adverse sanitation. These contrasts show why an income-only grouping cannot capture every dimension.

Profile numbers are ordered by median income only. They are not rankings of overall health or municipal performance. The table reports medians of municipal indicators.

Health resources outside the clustering

Health resources are external descriptive comparisons, not clustering inputs. Pooled rates sum jobs and population over the same observed municipalities. They answer a different question from the median municipal rate, and neither corrects for patients traveling across borders.

Adjusted values are correlations between rank residuals after linear adjustment for population, density and older-age share. They are not causal effects. Region-block intervals allow dependence inside each region but assume blocks are sufficiently independent; cross-border correlation remains possible. These are pointwise exploratory intervals, without correction across the full family of associations.

The UBS result is especially useful: differences per resident largely follow demographic context. A count of facilities does not capture their staffing, capacity, utilization or quality.

Comparison with a simple income grouping

Equal-frequency groups of median income provide a reference, with tied values kept together. The table measures in-sample variation explained in log1p health indicators. It must not be interpreted as prediction on unseen data. Clustering may add descriptive information for some resources, without universally outperforming income groups.

Geography and scale

Queen neighbors share at least one boundary vertex at seven decimal places. The graph has 1832 undirected edges and 1 isolated municipality (Ilhabela), excluded from Queen statistics but retained in maps and nearest-neighbor tests. The alternative graph symmetrizes each municipality’s six nearest polygon centroids on a unit sphere.

Global Moran statistics use 9,999 permutations, two-sided deviations from the permutation-null expectation, and BH adjustment over the eight global comparisons. Local income statistics use total randomization of all incomes, not conditional LISA permutations. The local test family has one municipality-level test per non-isolated municipality. BY correction is shown because it allows arbitrary dependence; BH is retained as a less conservative sensitivity.

Income, adverse sanitation and non-SUS physician resources exhibit positive spatial association. The SUS physician statistic is much weaker. Local income results include 13 municipalities under BH and 0 under BY at 5%. The main map therefore does not claim confirmed local hotspots. Conservative adjustment and limited permutation resolution reduce power.

Health-region tables pool resources and mortality, with explicit population coverage for missing professional records. This reduces fragmentation but does not measure referral flows, travel time or actual access. Conclusions can change with aggregation: an ecological association at one geographic scale need not hold at another.

Infant mortality: a secondary analysis

There are 134 municipalities with fewer than 100 live births in the pooled period and 118 with zero recorded infant deaths. Zero events do not demonstrate zero underlying risk. The quartile gradient and the near-zero municipal mean-income correlation coexist because pooling changes weighting and reduces count noise.

The numerator contains infant deaths in 2023–2024 and the denominator live births in those years, not a longitudinal birth cohort. Poisson intervals ignore overdispersion, spatial dependence and reporting uncertainty. Mortality does not select the profiles and is not used to claim a protective or harmful causal effect of resources.

Sensitivity, representative cases and limitations

The sensitivity table changes income definition, sanitation definition, transforms, extreme values, capital inclusion and population weights. Every alternative refits its scaler. Leave-one-health-region-out results are also exported. Individual stability aligns labels on the fitting subset with the Hungarian algorithm and counts agreement only when a municipality is excluded. It measures algorithmic sensitivity, not probability of a true group.

Representative cases are the two municipalities nearest each standardized profile center. Atypical cases are the five farthest from their assigned centers. This rule is explicit and describes feature-space geometry, not service need or policy priority.

  • Resource reference dates remain ambiguous. The denominator sensitivity compares 2023 and 2024 population, but cannot prove the underlying resource year.
  • Public snapshots can be revised. Frozen hashes support this analysis; fresh downloads require a new audit.
  • Municipal averages hide within-municipality inequality and do not establish individual-level relationships.
  • The limited feature set and modest sample support interpretable classical methods, not a claim of broad ML engineering or causal discovery.
  • High stability does not establish natural clusters; variable and weighting choices materially affect the typology.

Reproduce and inspect

Open this standalone report without a server. The notebook includes actual executed table outputs and embedded figures. The repository contains source snapshots, processed data, model centers, every candidate assignment, validation tables, tests and all nine figures.

python -m venv .venv
# Windows PowerShell: .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
# macOS/Linux: source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python run.py verify
python run.py run
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v

python run.py fetch restores missing source files only when live bytes match the frozen hash. python run.py fetch --refresh downloads current sources into a separate folder for review. Existing reference data are preserved. Equivalent Make targets are available, with no Unix-only shell commands.
